title: ExoPredicator: Learning Abstract Models of Dynamic Worlds for Robot Planning
claim: Real tasks need plans that interleave the agent's own actions with processes that unfold on their own over time.
layout: 1 wide panel, left-to-right timeline, color-coded Gantt bars above rendered frames
description: A wide horizontal strip with a black Time arrow across the top. At the far left, a labeled simulator scene shows a robot arm, faucet, faucet switch, jug, burner and burner switch, with the goal 'Goal: Boil Water'. To the right is an 'Abstract Plan' drawn like a Gantt chart. Teal boxes in the bottom row are the agent's endogenous actions: Switch on Faucet, Switch on Burner, Wait, Switch Off Faucet, Move Jug to Burner, Wait. Pink bars above them are exogenous processes that overlap those actions in time: Jug Filling with Water, Burner Preheating, Water Heating. Under each teal action is a rendered simulator frame. The jug fills with blue water, the burner turns orange, and the water finally turns red. The teal-versus-pink coding is what the eye lands on first.
caption: Dynamic environments include both endogenous processes (actions under the agent's direct control, such as Switch On Faucet) and exogenous processes (e.g., Jug Filling with Water) that evolve on their own. Planning requires reasoning about both kinds of processes.
abstract: Long-horizon embodied planning is challenging because the world does not only change through an agent's actions: exogenous processes (e.g., water heating, dominoes cascading) unfold concurrently with the agent's actions. We propose a framework for abstract world models that jointly learns (i) symbolic state representations and (ii) causal processes for both endogenous actions and exogenous mechanisms. Each causal process models the time course of a stochastic cause-effect relation. We learn these world models from limited data via variational Bayesian inference combined with LLM proposals. Across five simulated tabletop robotics environments, the learned models enable fast planning that generalizes to held-out tasks with more objects and more complex goals, outperforming a range of baselines.
